newsitem.title: UK: British economic boom won't rescue Major - analysts.
newsitem.headline: British economic boom won't rescue Major - analysts.

text.p: John Major looks likely to be the first British Prime Minister since the second World War to win an election during a recession and then lose one in the midst of an economic boom, analysts say.

Although Britain is enjoying the kind of sustained growth governments have dreamed of achieving for decades, few believe this nirvana can tempt disgruntled voters back to the ruling Conservatives in the May 1 general election.

But during the election campaign Major is hoping his soapbox oratory and the best economic conditions since the 1960s -- inflation falling towards 2.5 percent, growth rising above 3.0 percent and unemployment tumbling -- will win back support.

Conservatives hark back to the April 1992 election, which they won despite a deep and bitter recession. Now, the lively economic background -- to be highlighted this week by fresh inflation and unemployment data, could hardly be more promising.

But voting experts say the historic relationship between rising consumer confidence and government ratings may have snapped. The opposition Labour party under Tony Blair may simply end up inheriting a model economic upturn which could last a full parliamentary term, they predict.

The problem is the Conservatives have found it tough restoring their reputation for economic competence following the forced ejection of the pound out of Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) back in September 1992. At the same time, Labour's reputation has been improving while in opposition.

The dilemma was highlighted by a Reuters/NOP poll published Tuesday which found 35 percent of voters now trust Labour more to manage the economy, against 26 percent the Conservatives, even though Labour has been out of power since 1979.

"The economic upturn since 1992 has been largely due to our forced ejection from the ERM which the government tried to resist," said Jeremy Hawkins, analyst at Bank America. "Voters have been wary of crediting the government with the recovery."

So while the economy is booming, voters are reluctant to thank the Conservatives for the upturn and have warmed to Labour as its leadership moved away from the traditional tax-and-spend economic policies still favoured by many of its party activists.
The latest Reuters/NOP poll asked voters under which party they would be better off, taking into account what they spend, their taxes and their income from work, benefits and pensions.
Labour again registered a clear lead with 39 percent of voters backing them against 25 percent for the Conservatives.

And Labour's lead on this question was most marked in the skilled manual workers group, with a reading of 50 percent against 15 percent backing the Conservatives. The Conservatives only lead on the personal prosperity question among professional and managerial workers, by a margin of 20 percent.

The government is hoping, of course, that the much-heralded return of the "feel-good" factor -- consumers feeling more confident and spending more -- will eventually feed through to the polls before voting day. But evidence suggests Britons have already been feeling better -- according to confidence polls -- for at least the last two years, and this has not been accompanied by any significant upturn in Conservative support.

A Gallup poll at the end of 1996 showed voters remarkably optimistic, with 37 percent of people believing 1997 would be better than 1996 compared with just 21 percent who said it would be worse -- one of the strongest optimism readings this decade.

"The relationship between the feel good factor and Conservative voting intentions has clearly broken down and will not be re-established in the space of an election campaign," said Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident.

Ironically, while the strong economy will undoubtedly lure some voters back to the Conservatives, it may also have the perverse effect of making other voters more willing to take a risk with Labour, on the grounds the economy will continue to prosper whichever party is in power, analysts say.

In the April 1992 election, for example, many voters appeared wary of voting Labour (then associated with severe economic mismanagement in the 1970s) because the economy was mired in recession and the spectre of higher taxes and mortgage rates (associated with Labour) was uppermost in peoples' minds.

James Alt, in his book The Politics of Economic Decline, has argued that affluence was necessary for voters to feel economically secure enough to support leftist policies of social reform and higher social spending.

But voting experts reckon Labour still has to be wary as any undermining of its reputation on economic issues could do severe damage. The party has failed to score 40 percent of the vote in the past six elections, and still needs a large swing of around 4.1 percent in the coming election to capture power.
